faq.q: What size motorcycle is best for beginner touring?
faq.a: A 650-700cc bike is ideal for beginner touring in Britain. It provides enough power for motorway riding and overtaking while remaining manageable, fuel-efficient, and affordable to insure and maintain.

faq.q: Should I buy a new or used touring motorcycle as a beginner?
faq.a: I'd recommend buying a 2-3 year old used bike for your first tourer. You'll save thousands in depreciation while still getting a reliable machine with years of touring left in it, plus it often comes with luggage already fitted.

faq.q: Do I need an adventure bike or can I tour on a regular motorcycle?
faq.a: Adventure bikes suit British touring better due to mixed road surfaces, gravel car parks, and tight Scottish roads. However, bikes like the Ninja 650 or CBR650R can work well if you're sticking mainly to motorways and A-roads.

faq.q: How much should I budget for my first touring motorcycle setup?
faq.a: Budget £5,000-8,000 total including a used bike (£3,500-5,000), proper gear (£800), insurance (£300-800), luggage (£200-600), and accessories (£100-300). Don't forget running costs like servicing and tyres.

faq.q: What's more important: power or comfort for touring?
faq.a: Comfort wins every time. You'll be spending hours in the saddle on British roads. An upright riding position, manageable weight, and good wind protection matter far more than raw power for enjoyable touring.

faq.q: Can shorter riders handle touring motorcycles?
faq.a: Absolutely. Look for bikes with lower seat height options like the V-Strom 650 (available at 820mm), NC750X (800mm), or Versys 650. Being able to get both feet down confidently matters more than anything else.

Finding Your Perfect First Touring Bike: What I've Learned From Years on British Roads

I'll be straight with you—choosing your first touring motorcycle is one of the most important decisions you'll make as a rider. Get it right, and you'll spend years exploring Britain's incredible roads with a massive grin under your helmet. Get it wrong, and you'll be selling up within six months, frustrated and out of pocket.

I've been touring across Britain since 2018, and I've seen plenty of new riders make expensive mistakes. I've also seen plenty get it absolutely spot on. After riding everything from the A82 through Glencoe to the twisting lanes of the Welsh Marches, I've learned what actually matters in a touring bike for beginners. Let me share what I wish someone had told me when I started.

What Makes a Good Beginner Touring Motorcycle?

Before we dive into specific bikes, let's talk about what you actually need. Forget the marketing nonsense and the bloke down the pub who reckons you need a 1200cc adventure bike to ride to Scotland. Here's what genuinely matters when you're starting out.

Manageable Weight and Seat Height

I cannot stress this enough: if you can't comfortably hold your bike up at a standstill, you're going to have a miserable time. I've seen too many new riders tip over in car parks or struggle to get their bikes off the sidestand. Britain's touring routes often involve tight manoeuvring in pub car parks, narrow Scottish single-track roads, and slippery fuel station forecourts. You need confidence at low speeds.

Aim for something under 230kg wet weight if possible, and make sure you can get both feet flat on the ground. I'm 5'10" and I still prefer a lower seat height for touring—there's nothing worse than arriving at your B&B knackered after 300 miles and then having to tiptoe your bike into a tight spot.

Comfortable Riding Position

You'll be spending hours in the saddle. The A9 from Perth to Inverness alone can take five hours if you're doing it properly, stopping at viewpoints. A sportsbike crouch will leave you crippled. You want an upright position with slightly forward footpegs—think relaxed, not racer.

I learned this the hard way on a trip to the NC500. My mate was on an old sports tourer with clip-ons, and by day two he could barely turn his neck. Meanwhile, I was on something more upright and felt brilliant. Position matters more than power, trust me.

Weather Protection and Practicality

This is Britain. You will get wet. You'll be riding through Scottish mist, Welsh drizzle, and that horrible horizontal rain you get on the M6. A decent screen makes an enormous difference to your comfort and concentration. Hand guards are brilliant too—I fitted some to my bike after one particularly grim February ride through the Lake District.

You'll also need luggage capacity. Soft luggage works fine to start with, but make sure your bike has decent mounting points or a proper rack. I use gear from SportsBikeShop and they've never let me down, even in proper downpours.

The Best Beginner Touring Bikes for 2026

Right, let's get to the bikes. These are machines I've either ridden extensively myself or that mates I trust have toured on. Every one of these will do the job brilliantly for a new tourer.

Suzuki V-Strom 650

If there's a "default correct answer" for beginner touring, this is it. I've put thousands of miles on these bikes and they just work. The 650cc V-twin has enough power for motorway overtakes but won't scare you. The riding position is spot-on for all-day comfort. Weight is manageable at around 215kg, and the seat height, while tallish at 835mm, comes in a lower version.

I've ridden a V-Strom through everything Britain can throw at you. It handled the hairpins on the Bealach na Bà with ease, ate up the motorway miles to get there, and didn't complain when I hit gravel car parks at remote viewpoints. The 2026 models come with updated electronics including lean-sensitive ABS and decent traction control—stuff that genuinely helps in the wet.

Fuel economy is brilliant too. I regularly get 55-60 mpg, which means you can do nearly 200 miles between fills. That's perfect for Scottish touring where petrol stations can be sparse.

Kawasaki Versys 650

The Versys is the V-Strom's main rival and it's equally excellent. Slightly more road-focused, a bit more nimble in the bends, and with a great aftermarket luggage scene. The parallel twin engine is smooth and willing, and the adjustable screen is genuinely useful.

I've borrowed one for a week-long tour through Wales and loved it. The handling on roads like the A470 through the Brecon Beacons was absolutely superb—planted and confidence-inspiring even when pushing on a bit. At 216kg it's easy to manhandle in tight spots, and the narrow profile means filtering through traffic is a breeze.

Honda NC750X

Here's a wildcard that deserves serious consideration. The NC750X is brilliant for beginners because it's so completely unstressable. The engine is smooth rather than exciting, but it has enough grunt for touring and the fuel economy is frankly ridiculous—I've seen 75 mpg on gentle rides.

What I love about the NC is the storage where the fuel tank usually sits. You can fit a full-face helmet in there, which is genius for overnight stops. The DCT automatic gearbox option divides opinion, but I know several touring riders who swear by it, especially in heavy traffic or after a long day when you're tired.

It's also one of the cheapest bikes to insure and maintain, which matters when you're starting out and money's tight.

Yamaha Tracer 7

If you want something a bit more sporting without sacrificing touring capability, the Tracer 7 is superb. The CP2 parallel twin engine is a joy—loads of character, great sound, and enough punch to make overtaking effortless. The chassis is genuinely good fun on twisty roads.

I've ridden the Tracer 7 on some of Britain's best roads, including the Isle of Skye to the Highlands route, and it was absolutely in its element. Comfortable enough for the long hauls, but proper entertaining on the good bits. At 196kg it's one of the lighter options too.

The 2026 model gets cruise control as standard, which is brilliant for those long motorway slogs. The screen could be taller, but aftermarket options are readily available.

Triumph Tiger 660 Sport

Triumph's new middleweight adventure tourer is a cracking bike. The 660cc triple engine is smooth, characterful, and makes a gorgeous noise. Build quality is excellent, the electronics package is comprehensive, and it looks fantastic.

It's at the pricier end for a beginner bike, but if budget allows, it's worth considering. I've done a long-term test on one and the comfort levels are exceptional. The seat is wide and supportive, the bars are well-positioned, and the wind protection is decent.

One thing to note: at 206kg it's light and manageable, but the seat height of 835mm might be a stretch for shorter riders. Triumph offers a lower seat option though.

Royal Enfield Himalayan 450

For riders who want something different and don't need to rush, the new Himalayan 450 is genuinely good. I was sceptical at first—old Royal Enfields had quality issues—but this new generation is properly sorted.

It's light at 196kg, simple to maintain, affordable to buy and run, and has charm by the bucketload. The engine isn't powerful, but it's smooth and torquey enough for British roads. I wouldn't want to do five hours on the M6, but for touring Scotland or Wales on A and B roads, it's lovely.

The upright position is perfect for all-day riding, and the basic nature of the bike means you're not worried about expensive plastics when you drop it in a muddy car park. Because let's be honest, at some point you probably will.

The perfect beginner touring bike isn't the one with the most power or the flashiest tech—it's the one that makes you want to ride it every weekend, that fits your body, and that you can afford to run without breaking the bank.

What About Adventure Bikes vs Sport Tourers?

This is a question I get asked constantly. Here's my take: for Britain, adventure bikes make more sense for most riders. Our roads are mixed—you'll do motorways, A-roads, B-roads, and sometimes gravel car parks or muddy field camping. Adventure bikes handle all of this brilliantly.

Sport tourers like the Yamaha FJR1300 or BMW R1250RT are fantastic machines, but they're heavy, expensive, and often overpowered for beginners. They're also completely wrong for tight Scottish single-track roads or Welsh mountain passes where you need manoeuvrability.

That said, if you're planning to do mostly motorway miles and bigger A-roads, something like a Kawasaki Ninja 650 or Honda CBR650R with luggage can work well. They're comfortable enough for touring, lighter than full sport tourers, and less intimidating for new riders.

Essential Features to Look For

Beyond the specific bike models, here's what I'd be checking off the list:

  • ABS: Non-negotiable. British roads are slippery from October to April, and emergency stops on wet Scottish A-roads are terrifying without it.
  • Adjustable screen: Even a few centimetres make a huge difference to wind protection and comfort.
  • Standard luggage mounts: Makes life so much easier than bodging on soft luggage.
  • Heated grips: Not essential but bloody lovely. Riding the A9 in March without them is grim.
  • Decent fuel range: 150+ miles minimum. Petrol stations are rare in the Highlands.
  • Service intervals: Look for 6,000-mile or longer intervals. More time riding, less time at the dealer.
  • Aftermarket support: Popular bikes have better luggage options, screen choices, and protective accessories.

New vs Used: What I'd Recommend

Here's the thing—buying new is lovely but you lose thousands in depreciation the moment you ride away. For a first touring bike, I'd seriously consider used. A three-year-old V-Strom 650 or Versys 650 will have lost a chunk of value but still has years of reliable touring left in it.

What I'd look for in a used touring bike:

  • Full service history—absolutely essential
  • Low to average mileage (touring bikes often rack up miles, but well-maintained high-mileage bikes can be fine)
  • No crash damage—check carefully around mirrors, bar ends, and engine cases
  • Original owner documents and V5C logbook
  • Evidence of regular chain maintenance and tyre changes

I bought my current bike at two years old with 8,000 miles on it. Saved nearly £3,000 versus new, and it came with luggage already fitted. Best decision I made.

Budget Considerations Beyond the Bike

Don't forget you'll need gear and running costs. Here's what I budget for:

  • Insurance: £300-800 depending on age, location, and bike choice
  • Gear: £800+ for proper jacket, trousers, boots, gloves, and helmet
  • Luggage: £200-600 depending on whether you go soft bags or hard cases
  • Accessories: £100-300 for things like phone mounts, USB sockets, tank bag
  • First service: £150-300
  • Chain and sprockets: £150-250 every 15,000-20,000 miles
  • Tyres: £200-350 every 6,000-10,000 miles

Use the trip planning tool to work out your actual touring costs including accommodation and fuel. It helps you budget properly and avoid nasty surprises.

Learning to Tour: Start Small

Don't plan a three-week NC500 trip for your first tour. Start with overnighters. Ride 150 miles, stay somewhere nice, ride home. You'll learn what works and what doesn't without committing to a massive journey.

I started with weekend trips to the Peak District and Yorkshire Dales. Learned how to pack efficiently, worked out my comfortable daily mileage (around 250-300 miles for me), and figured out what gear I actually needed versus what I thought I needed.

The packing checklist tool is brilliant for this—it helps you avoid overpacking, which every new tourer does at least once. Trust me, you don't need three pairs of shoes for a weekend trip.

My Honest Recommendation

If I was buying my first touring bike tomorrow with my own money, I'd get a used Suzuki V-Strom 650 or Kawasaki Versys 650. Both are proven, reliable, comfortable, and capable. Parts are cheap, mechanics know them, and they hold value reasonably well.

They'll take you anywhere in Britain without breaking a sweat. I've ridden both on everything from motorways to mountain passes, in sunshine and storms, and they just crack on with the job. They're not exciting or glamorous, but they're brilliant tools for exploring this incredible island of ours.

That said, the "best" bike is the one that fits you and your budget. Sit on everything, test ride what you can, and be honest about your actual needs versus your wants. Don't buy a bike because it looks cool in photos—buy it because it feels right when you're riding it.

Getting Started: Your Action Plan

Right, enough reading. Here's what you should do next:

  • Set a realistic budget including bike, gear, insurance, and accessories
  • Visit dealers and sit on the bikes I've mentioned—don't skip this step
  • Book test rides on your top three choices
  • Check insurance quotes before you fall in love with something unaffordable
  • Read owner forums for real-world experiences and common issues
  • Plan your first short tour using the route builder to give yourself a goal

The roads are waiting. Britain has some of the finest motorcycle touring in the world—dramatic Scottish Highlands, flowing Welsh valleys, stunning Lake District passes, and endless beautiful B-roads. Get yourself sorted with the right bike and get out there. You won't regret it.

I'll see you out there. Give me a nod if you pass a scruffy bloke on a V-Strom covered in Scottish midges.
